did.unittitle: John E. Herzog collection of women's financial ephemera
did.abstract: This collection includes a selection of ephemera documenting American women's involvement in business and finance over more than 170 years. The bulk of the collection consists of stock certificates, many for businesses or organizations run by women or associated with women.
did.physloc: Materials in this collection may be stored offsite. For more information on making arrangements to consult them, please visit www.nyhistory.org/library/visit.
did.langmaterial: The documents in the collection are in English.

arrangement.head: Arrangement
arrangement.p:
The collection is organized into 8 series:
I. Autographs and letters
II. Circulars and handbills
III. Commemorative envelopes and stamps
IV. Engravings, illustrations, and photographs
V. Membership certificates
VI. Miscellaneous financial documents
VII. Stock certificates
VIII. Supporting ephemera

bioghist.head: Biographical / Historical
bioghist.p: This collection was compiled by John E. Herzog, the founder of the Museum of American Finance. Herzog was born in New York City in 1936 to Robert I. Herzog and Norma (Englander) Herzog. His father, Robert I. Herzog, founded the bond trading and brokerage company Parmer, Herzog & Chadwick that later became Herzog Heine Geduld, a firm specializing in NASDAQ and OTC securities. John E. Herzog received his B.A. in Economics from Cornell University in 1957 and his M.B.A. from Stern School of Business at New York University in 1971. He married Diana E. Rigby in 1963, and the couple had two daughters, Mary and Sarah.

Herzog was Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of Herzog Heine Geduld, Inc.; a member of the Board of Overseers at the Leonard N. Stern School of Business at NYU; and Chairman of Spink/Smythe, an auction house which specialized in antique stocks and bonds, bank notes, autographs and photographs. After the stock market crash of 1987, he founded the Museum of American Finance to improve public understanding of finance and economic history. The Museum of American Finance, formerly located in the Financial District in New York City, recently moved to a new location in Boston.

processinfo.p: Items were rehoused in archival folders. The sleeves housing the items were retained because many include labels indicating where the items were purchased.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: This collection documents American women's involvement in business and finance over more than 170 years. The bulk of the collection consists of stock certificates, many for businesses or organizations run by women or associated with women. Women's education is covered by stock certificates for a wide range of schools, including the Female Collegiate Institute in Virginia, Albany Female Academy in New York, Brownsville Female College in Tennessee, and others. Other stock certificates highlight women's clothing and appearance, including the Co-operative Dress Association, The Reece Button Hole Machine Company, McLean & Hooper Sewing Machine Company, the Norfolk and New Brunswick Hosiery Company, and the American Beauty Culture Society. Women's health is represented by stock certificates for American Gynecology and the Vaginette Surgical Instrument Company.

The collection also shows women participating in fields typically dominated by men. A number of stock certificates show the growing range of publishers for women: The Ladies' Home Magazine Publishing Company, Woman Patriot Publishing Company, Western Woman's World Publishing Company, etc. Women are also involved in real estate, demonstrated by new companies like the American Women's Realty Corporation, the Woman's Land Syndicate, and the San Francisco Women's Building Association. Women are even founding new mining companies, like Mollie E. O'Bryan's Teutonic Consolidated Gold Mines Company in Wyoming and the Transvaal Gold Mining Company in Colorado. There are several examples of women buying stock in railroad companies, including a stock certificate for the Panama Rail Road Company issued to Harriet Beecher Stowe. There is also a circular for an oil company run by a woman, The Woman's Right Oil & Gas Co. of Okmulgee, Oklahoma.

Many items in the collection focus on the major 19th- and early 20th-century women's movements of temperance and suffrage. Numerous stock certificates and other ephemera document the temperance movement, including the Union Temperance League of Ohio, the Lincoln Temperance Association, the Women's Christian Temperance Union of Pennsylvania, and the National Women's Christian Temperance Union. Herzog has collected autograph notes and other ephemera from many of the big names in these movements, including Harriet Beecher Stowe, Julia Ward Howe, Susan B. Anthony, Alice Stone Blackwell, Elizabeth Cady Stanton, Frances E. Willard, and others. He also includes engravings or photographs of many of these women.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p:
• Julia Ward Howe autograph cards and notes, including two lines of verse with her signature, November 23, 1879; her calling card with her signature, April 12, 1882; and an autograph note signed to "Dear [A.B.R.?]", November 28, 1905, in which she says she will not be able to attend either of the Garrison meetings because she is "under orders for the present to avoid all fatigues of that kind, as they are apt to give [her] an attack of painful dizziness"
• Payment from the National-American Woman Suffrage Association to The Tribune Company for $5.75 for printing on December 31, 1897. Signed by Susan B. Anthony, President, and Alice Stone Blackwell, Rec. Sec'y. Also includes a postcard of John Howe Kent's photograph of Mary and Susan B. Anthony
• Elizabeth Cady Stanton signed quotation, "Work is worship" R[alph] W[aldo] E[merson] / Elizabeth Cady Stanton / N.Y. March 1st, 1873, with a reproduction of a Sarony photograph of Stanton and an engraving of her by H.B. Hall, Jr., N.Y.
• Document signed by Harriet Beecher Stowe appointing her attorney, John T. Howard, to sell her Panama Railroad Company stock for her, January 9, 1872, with an engraving of Stowe by J.A.J. Wilson
• Autograph letter signed from Frances E. Willard to Sen. L.M. Morrill, Evanston, January 13, 1879, asking him to support the "Home Protection" campaign, on letterhead stationery of the Women's Christian Temperance Union of Illinois; also includes a stock certificate for Temperance Hall, Northern Liberties, no. 199 issued to George S. Shugart, October 4, 1839 and Woman's Christian Temperance Union honorary member pledge card signed by Ambrose L. Walk

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p:
• Circular for The Woman's Right Oil & Gas Co., Okmulgee, Oklahoma, 1917, accompanied by a typed letter from H.C. Kessler to Mr. E.A. Hill dated April 7, 1917: "inclosed [sic] you will find circular letter Mrs. Kessler is now in the oil game if you can do any good for the cause do so. drop one of these circular's [sic] where it will sprout and grow."
• Union handbill published for the National Woman's Christian Temperance Union by the National Temperance Society and Publication House, New York: "How Much Is Your Boy Worth?", no. 45, Gospel Series
• Handbill in which one side is a facsimile of $10 in Confederate currency and the other side reads, "I will give $1000 in gold if I fail to cure any cancer or tumor … Any lump in woman's breast is cancer and if neglected, it always poisons deep in the armpit and kills quickly. For this valuable free book, address Dr. and Mrs. Dr. Chamley, Managers, Chamley Home, Offices, 747 So. Main St., Los Angeles, Cal., U.S.A.", [18--?]

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Includes supplemental materials related to famous women such as newspaper and magazine clippings, printouts of journal articles, flyers, postcards, brochures, and other ephemera.
